source: Office of the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks (CGPDTM)
section: Section 2(1)(j) & Section 3 — Patentable Subject Matter & Statutory Exclusions
content: Under Section 2(1)(j) of the Indian Patents Act, 1970, an invention means a new product or process involving an inventive step and capable of industrial application. An inventive step requires a feature involving technical advance or economic significance making it non-obvious to a person skilled in the art. Section 3 lists non-patentable inventions: Section 3(a) frivolous inventions contrary to natural laws; Section 3(b) commercial exploitation contrary to public order or morality; Section 3(c) mere discovery of scientific principle or abstract theory; Section 3(d) mere discovery of a new form of a known substance without enhancement of known efficacy; Section 3(e) mere admixture resulting in only aggregation of properties; Section 3(f) mere arrangement or rearrangement of known devices; Section 3(h) method of agriculture or horticulture; Section 3(i) medicinal, surgical, curative, prophylactic or diagnostic methods; Section 3(j) plants and animals in whole or part other than micro-organisms; Section 3(k) mathematical, business method, computer program per se or algorithms; Section 3(p) an invention which in effect is traditional knowledge or an aggregation or duplication of known properties of traditionally known components.

source: Office of the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks (CGPDTM)
section: Chapter III & Rules — Patent Filing Procedure and Mandatory Forms
content: To file a patent application in India, the applicant must file Form 1 (Application for Grant of Patent) along with Form 2 (Provisional or Complete Specification). A Provisional Specification secures priority date, and Complete Specification must be filed within 12 months. Form 3 (Statement and Undertaking under Section 8 regarding foreign applications) must be submitted within 6 months of filing. Form 5 (Declaration as to Inventorship) is required with complete specification. Patent publication occurs automatically 18 months from filing/priority date under Section 11A. Early publication can be requested via Form 9 within 1 month. Substantive examination is not automatic; Form 18 (Request for Examination) must be filed within 48 months from priority/filing date. Startups, small entities, and female natural persons qualify for expedited examination via Form 18A under Rule 24C. Indian residents must obtain Section 39 permission or file first in India 6 weeks before filing foreign patents.

source: Office of the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks (CGPDTM)
section: Section 53 — Term of Patent and Statutory Validity
content: Under Section 53 of the Indian Patents Act, 1970 (as amended), the term of every patent granted in India is 20 years from the date of filing of the application. In cases of international applications filed under the Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) designating India, the 20-year term is computed from the international filing date. To maintain a patent in force throughout its 20-year validity, renewal fees must be paid annually starting before the expiration of the 2nd year from the date of the patent. If the renewal fee is not paid within the prescribed period (or 6-month extension under Section 142), the patent lapses under Section 53(2), though restoration may be applied for within 18 months from cessation under Section 60.

section: Sections 2(1)(zb), 9 & 11 — Trademark Meaning, Absolute & Relative Grounds for Refusal
content: Under Section 2(1)(zb) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, a trade mark means a mark capable of being represented graphically and capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of others, and may include shape of goods, packaging, and combination of colours. Trademarks are classified under the international Nice Classification into 45 classes (Classes 1-34 for goods, Classes 35-45 for services). For example, Class 5 covers pharmaceuticals, veterinary preparations, and Ayurvedic medicinal formulations. Section 9 outlines Absolute Grounds for Refusal: marks devoid of distinctive character, marks indicating kind, quality, quantity, intended purpose, or geographical origin. Section 11 outlines Relative Grounds for Refusal: identity or deceptive similarity to an earlier trade mark and similarity of goods/services creating a likelihood of confusion among the public.

section: Trade Marks Rules 2017 — Filing and Registration Procedure
content: Trademark application is filed online through Form TM-A with the Trade Marks Registry. The application must specify the applicant details, mark representation, class of goods/services, and whether the mark is in use (with user date affidavit) or proposed to be used. Following filing, the Registry issues an Examination Report within 1 to 3 months. If objections under Section 9 or Section 11 are raised, a written response must be submitted within 30 days. If the Registrar is satisfied or following a show-cause hearing, the mark is advertised in the Trade Marks Journal. A 4-month statutory opposition period begins under Section 21. If no opposition is received or opposition is dismissed, the Registrar issues a Certificate of Registration under Section 23.

section: Section 25 — Duration, Validity, and Renewal of Trademark
content: Under Section 25 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999, the registration of a trade mark is valid for a period of 10 years from the date of application. Unlike patents which expire after 20 years and enter the public domain, a trademark registration can be renewed indefinitely every 10 years by filing Form TM-R along with the prescribed fee. Renewal can be filed at any time within 1 year before the expiration of the last registration. If a trademark is not renewed, the Registrar sends notice Form O-3, and if unpaid, removes the mark from the Register, though restoration is possible within 1 year of expiration under Section 25(4).

source: Copyright Office, Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT)
section: Sections 13, 14 & 22 — Scope, Economic Rights, and Term of Copyright Protection
content: Under Section 13 of the Copyright Act, 1957, copyright subsists throughout India in original literary, dramatic, musical, and artistic works, cinematograph films, and sound recordings. Computer programs and software code are protected as literary works under Section 2(o). Copyright vests automatically upon creation without mandatory registration, though registration under Chapter X provides prima facie evidentiary proof in court. Under Section 22, the general term of copyright protection for published literary, dramatic, musical, and artistic works is the lifetime of the author plus 60 years computed from the year following the author's death. For anonymous works, cinematograph films, sound recordings, and government works, the term is 60 years from publication.

source: Geographical Indications Registry of India, Chennai
section: Sections 2(e), 8 & 18 — Meaning, Registration, and Validity of Geographical Indications
content: Under Section 2(e) of the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, a Geographical Indication (GI) identifies agricultural, natural, or manufactured goods originating in the territory of a country, or a region/locality in that territory, where a given quality, reputation, or other characteristic of such goods is essentially attributable to its geographical origin. Any association of persons or producers representing the interest of the producers can apply under Form GI-1. The GI registry records both the Registered Proprietor and Authorized Users under Form GI-3. Under Section 18, GI registration is valid for 10 years and can be renewed indefinitely for successive periods of 10 years. Prominent Indian GIs include Darjeeling Tea (GI No. 1), Tirupati Laddu, Pochampally Ikat, Kangra Tea, Alphonso Mango, and Kashmiri Pashmina. GI rights prevent unauthorized parties from exploiting the geographical reputation.

section: Sections 2(d), 4 & 11 — Industrial Design Protectable Features, Novelty, and Term
content: Under Section 2(d) of the Designs Act, 2000, 'design' means only the features of shape, configuration, pattern, ornament or composition of lines or colours applied to any article by any industrial process, whether manual, mechanical, or chemical, which in the finished article appeal to and are judged solely by the eye. It expressly excludes any mode or principle of construction, mere mechanical devices, trade marks, and artistic works protected under Copyright. Under Section 4, a design must be new or original, not previously published in India or abroad, and significantly distinguishable from known designs. Under Section 11, the copyright in a registered industrial design is valid initially for 10 years from the date of registration, extendable by an additional 5 years upon filing Form 3 before the expiration of the initial 10-year period, providing a total maximum protection of 15 years.

source: Council of Scientific & Industrial Research (CSIR) & Ministry of AYUSH
content: The Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) is a pioneer initiative by CSIR and the Ministry of AYUSH codifying over 4.5 lakh formulations from classical Ayurvedic treatises (Charaka Samhita, Sushruta Samhita, Ashtanga Hridaya), Unani, Siddha, and Sowa-Rigpa in five international languages (English, German, French, Japanese, Spanish) classified under International Patent Classification (IPC Class A61K 36). Under Section 3(p) of the Patents Act 1970, inventions that are traditional knowledge or aggregations of known properties are barred from patentability. Classical formulations documented in TKDL act as anticipatory prior art. Worldwide patent offices (USPTO, EPO, JPO, IPO) consult TKDL to reject wrongful biopiracy patents. To overcome Section 3(p) scrutiny, patent applicants must demonstrate unexpected synergistic efficacy (Combination Index < 0.8), non-obvious bio-enhancement ratios, or novel pharmaceutical delivery formulations (e.g. liposomal or nano-carriers).

section: Sections 3, 6 & 7 — Mandatory Form III Approval for Intellectual Property on Indian Bio-resources
content: Under Section 6 of the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 (amended by Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act 2023), no person shall apply for any intellectual property right, by whatever name called, in or outside India for any invention based on any research or information on a biological resource obtained from India, without obtaining the prior approval of the National Biodiversity Authority (NBA). The applicant must submit Form III along with the prescribed fee before the patent is granted by the Indian Patent Office (IPO). Under Section 3, foreign entities, non-resident Indians (NRIs), and companies with foreign participation must obtain Form I approval before accessing any Indian biological resource. Indian citizens accessing biological resources for commercial utilization must give prior intimation to the concerned State Biodiversity Board (SBB) under Section 7. Failure to obtain NBA clearance can lead to refusal, revocation of the patent, and penal sanctions.

source: Ministry of AYUSH & Central Drugs Standard Control Organization (CDSCO)
section: Rule 158B — Licensing Regulatory Pathways for Classical vs Proprietary ASU Medicines
content: Under Rule 158B of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945, manufacturing licenses for Ayurveda, Siddha, and Unani (ASU) medicines are bifurcated into two distinct regulatory pathways: (1) Classical ASU Drugs (Shastriya): Formulations manufactured strictly according to the recipes codified in the authoritative texts listed in the First Schedule of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 (e.g. Charaka Samhita, Sharangadhara Samhita, Bhasishajya Ratnavali). These do not require animal safety or clinical trial data dossiers for licensing by the State AYUSH Licensing Authority. (2) Proprietary ASU Medicines (Anubhuta): Novel combinations or modified ratios of traditional ingredients. Under Rule 158B(IV), proprietary ASU medicines require proof of safety and effectiveness, including published literature on safety, acute oral toxicity data, and three-batch pilot stability data complying with Rule 161 heavy metal (lead, cadmium, arsenic, mercury) and microbial load limits.
